food.text: Pontic Olbia was a Greek city on the Southern Bug estuary in Ukraine, founded in the 7th century BC by colonists from Miletus. Its harbour was one of the main emporia on the Black Sea. It exported cereals, fish and slaves to Greece and imported Attic goods to Scythia.

The most important export of the north Black Sea coast was grain, especially wheat. Its importance grew in the later 6th century BC, when the Persian Empire conquered Egypt. That conquest deprived the states of Greece proper of the Egyptian grain they depended on.
Winemaking on the Don emerged with the appearance of the first Greek colonies, approximately in the sixth century B.C.E. Wine later became a traditional alcoholic beverage of the Don Cossacks.

Satyrus, who ruled from 431 to 387 BC, besieged the city of Theodosia. It was wealthy because, unlike other cities in the region, its port was free of ice all year. That let it trade grain with the rest of the Greek world even in winter.

In the early 5th century BC the Scythians destroyed the Greek cities' khōrai and rural settlements, wrecking their grain-producing hinterlands. The Greek colonies shifted from agricultural production to trading grain produced elsewhere. The Scythian monopoly on grain imported from the forest steppe ended sometime between 435 and 400 BC.

In the 4th century AD, Ammianus Marcellinus wrote that the Cherronesus (modern Crimea), on the left shore of the Maeotis (modern Sea of Azov), was densely settled with Greek colonies. He emphasized that, as a result, its inhabitants were calm and peaceful, farming the land and living off its produce. In contrast, he described the nearby Tauri tribes as exceptionally cruel and ruthless.
The ancient Greek historian Strabo wrote that he visited the mouth of the Don, where the vines were covered with earth for the winter. This protected them from snow and frost.

art.text: Starting from the 8th century BC, numerous Greek colonies appeared on the northern Black Sea coast. The most prominent were Tyras, Olbia, Chersonesus, Theodosia and Panticapaeum, now Kerch. The first monuments of stone architecture in what is now Ukraine date from this period of Antiquity.
Nomadic tribes of the southern lands in the 4th century BCE, such as the Scythians, produced finely worked gold ornaments. One example is the pectoral found in the Tovsta Mohyla mound.

The architecture of the early Greek settlements on the Black Sea coast was strongly influenced by the building traditions of Ionia, from which many of the colonists came. Starting from the 5th century BC, Athenian influence became obvious in the region.
Among the valuable structures preserved from the era of Greek colonization in modern-day Ukraine are ruins of defensive walls, residential houses and temples. Elements of columns also survive.

Hellenistic architecture became widespread in the Pontic area during the first centuries of the new era. This came after Ionian and then Athenian influences had shaped the Greek colonies on the northern Black Sea coast.

war.text: In 513 BC, Darius I of the Achaemenid Empire crossed the Bosphorus Straits on a bridge of boats and marched against the Scythians. The Scythians avoided a direct fight and laid waste to the countryside with a scorched earth tactic, and the Persians suffered losses. After chasing them for a month, Darius's army was suffering from fatigue, privation and sickness, and he ended up with very heavy losses and no territorial gains.

The Scythians were nomads skilled in mounted warfare. In the 8th century BC they displaced the Agathyrsi and the Cimmerians as the dominant power on the western Eurasian Steppe. They remained on the Pontic Steppe, in modern Ukraine and Southern Russia, until the 3rd century BC.

In the late 4th century AD, Alans and Huns moving west from the east overwhelmed the Goths living in present-day Ukraine, and many Goths gathered at the Lower Danube seeking refuge inside the Roman Empire. Mistreated by corrupt local Roman officials, the refugees soon starved, and some were reportedly forced to sell their children to Roman slave traders in return for rotten dog meat. Enraged, Fritigern led a widescale rebellion in Thrace, joined by Gothic refugees and slaves, Roman workers and peasants, and Gothic deserters from the Roman army. The Gothic War culminated in the Battle of Adrianople in 378, where the Romans were badly defeated and the emperor Valens was killed.

Darius's army chased the Scythians deep into what is now Ukraine, where there were no cities to conquer and no supplies to forage. The Scythians retreated eastwards, laying waste to the countryside with feints, skirmishes, blocked wells, intercepted convoys and destroyed pastures. While moving east, Darius captured Gelonos, the large fortified city of the Budini, allies of the Scythians, and burnt it. After a month of pursuit his army was suffering losses from fatigue, privation and sickness.

Late in the 4th century BC, the Macedonian kings Philip II of Macedon and Lysimachus defeated the Scythians in 339 and 313 BC. Weakened, the Scythians came under pressure from the Thracian Getae and the Celtic Bastarnae. Taking advantage, the Sarmatians crossed the Don river and invaded Scythia.

In the 1st century AD, the Sarmatians began encroaching on the Roman Empire in alliance with Germanic tribes. In the 3rd century AD, the Germanic Goths broke Sarmatian dominance of the Pontic Steppe. After the Hunnic invasions of the 4th century, many Sarmatians joined the Goths and settled in the Western Roman Empire.

Frustrated, Darius sent a letter to the Scythian ruler Idanthyrsus demanding that he fight or surrender. Idanthyrsus replied that he would not stand and fight unless the Persians found and desecrated the graves of the Scythians' forefathers. Until then, the Scythians would continue their strategy, since they had no cities or cultivated lands to lose.

Almost everything known about Darius's Scythian campaign comes from Herodotus's book The Histories. Almost no Persian sources exist, and no Scythian ones, so it is difficult to know how much of his account is accurate.

In 332, Constantine helped the Sarmatians settle on the north banks of the Danube to defend against Gothic attacks. Around 100,000 Goths were reportedly killed in battle, and Aoric, son of the Thervingian king Ariaric, was captured. From 335 to 336, Constantine continued his Danube campaign and defeated many Gothic tribes.

The Scythians across the Sea are mentioned at Naqsh-e Rustam as a people the Persian king conquered. János Harmatta thought the expedition had actually annexed Scythia. In his view, the Scythians freed themselves only in 496 BC, when the Achaemenids lost all their European territories due to the Ionian Revolt.

Excavations of the Early Sarmatian Filippovka kurgan, dated to about 450 to 300 BC, have uncovered numerous weapons, armour and helmets. The finds give a glimpse of the equipment of the mounted Sarmatian warriors who came to dominate the Pontic steppe.

The historian Eusebius wrote that in 334, Constantine evacuated approximately 300,000 Sarmatians from the north bank of the Danube. This followed a revolt of the Sarmatians' slaves. It shows how unstable the frontier with the Goths and Sarmatians was.

literature.text: Among the notable finds at Pontic Olbia, a Greek city on the Southern Bug estuary in modern Ukraine, is a private letter written on a lead tablet. It dates to around 500 BCE and complains about an attempt to claim a slave.

The Roman poet Ovid was exiled by Augustus to Tomis on the Black Sea, where he stayed for the last nine or 10 years of his life. He blamed his banishment on a carmen et error, a "poem and a mistake", but never gave specifics, which has led to much speculation among scholars.

For his Bible translation into the Gothic language, the 4th-century bishop Ulfilas developed the Gothic alphabet. It was largely based on the Greek alphabet, with Latin and Runic characters also used.
During the 5th century BCE the Greek colony of Pontic Olbia was visited by Herodotus. He provides the best description of the city and its inhabitants that survives from antiquity.
The Roman poet Ovid, during his long exile in Tomis, is said to have written poetry in the Getic language. That poetry is now lost.

Ovid's five books of Tristia, dated to AD 9–12, are poems expressing his despair in exile and pleading for his return to Rome. The Epistulae ex Ponto, letters to friends in Rome asking them to help him return, are thought to be his last compositions.

Gothic is known mainly from the Codex Argenteus, a 6th-century copy of a 4th-century Bible translation. It is the earliest Germanic language attested in any sizable texts, and the only East Germanic language with a sizeable text corpus.

Ovid describes the people of Tomis differently in his two exile works. In the Tristia they are frightening barbarians, but in the Epistulae he claims friendship with them and says he wrote a poem in their language.
The Gothic Bible has traditionally been credited to Ulfila alone. Analysis of its text, however, indicates that a team of translators was involved, possibly working under his supervision.
A few Gothic runic inscriptions have been found across Europe. Because the Goths were Christianized early, runic writing was quickly replaced by the newly invented Gothic alphabet.
In his Epistulae ex Ponto, written from the northern coast of the Black Sea, Ovid asserts that two major, distinct languages were spoken by the tribes of Scythia. He called them Getic and Sarmatian.

The main account of Ulfila's life is a 4th-century letter by his pupil Auxentius of Durostorum, written right after his death. In the 5th century the Arian theologian Maximinus copied it into the margins of one copy of Ambrose's De Fide.

politics.text: During the Iron Age, nomadic peoples such as the Cimmerians, Scythians and Sarmatians lived in what is now Ukraine. The Scythian kingdom existed there from 750 to 250 BC.

In 513 BC, the Achaemenid Persian army of Darius the Great campaigned into Scythia. It subjugated several Thracian peoples and virtually all other regions along the European part of the Black Sea before it returned to Asia Minor.

Greeks, mostly from the city-state of Miletus, colonized large parts of Crimea and the Sea of Azov during the seventh and sixth centuries BC. They were eventually unified into the Bosporan Kingdom by 480 BC.
In 107 BC the Bosporan Kingdom was incorporated into the large Kingdom of Pontus. The Roman Republic later conquered that kingdom, and the Bosporan Kingdom became a client state of the Roman Empire.
From 62 to 68 AD the Roman Empire briefly annexed the Bosporan Kingdom under Emperor Nero. Nero had deposed the Bosporan king Tiberius Julius Cotys I.
In the 3rd and 4th centuries AD, a semi-legendary Gothic kingdom of Oium existed in Southern Russia until it was overrun by Huns. The Goths had migrated to the Black Sea at about the 2nd century AD.

The Achaemenid Empire was the largest empire of its time, at its peak roughly 5.5 million square kilometres. Yet it was repulsed from Scythia in 513 BC, as well as from Greece in 492–490 BC and 480–479 BC.
After the brief annexation under Nero, the Bosporan Kingdom was made into a Roman client state. It hosted a Roman military presence during the middle of the 1st century AD.
The culturally Greek Bosporan Kingdom thrived for centuries. It was finally invaded and occupied by the Goths and Huns in the 4th century AD.

Between the 3rd and 6th centuries AD, the Bosporan Kingdom was overwhelmed by successive waves of nomadic invasions. These were led by warlike tribes, such as the Huns and Turkish Avars, which often moved on to Europe.

philosophy.text: Herodotus, writing before 425 BC, described Zalmoxis as a divinity of the Getae and Dacians, peoples of the lower Danube. Jordanes' Getica later called him a learned philosopher, preceded by two other learned men named Zeuta and Deceneus.

Anacharsis was a Scythian prince and philosopher of uncertain historicity who lived in the 6th century BC. Later Graeco-Roman tradition made him a symbol of 'Barbarian wisdom', and the ancient Greeks included him among the Seven Sages of Greece.

During the 5th century BCE, Greek colonists in Thrace connected Zalmoxis to the philosopher Pythagoras. They saw similar prophetic abilities and magical healing, and they noticed that Getic nobles feasted together in banqueting halls much as Pythagorean adepts met and ate in common halls.

Strabo wrote that King Burebista (82–44 BC) hired Deceneus, a man who had been in Egypt, to 'tame' his people. As a sign of obedience, the people agreed to destroy all their wines at his order. Strabo calls Deceneus a 'magician'.

The 6th-century historian Jordanes described Deceneus teaching the Getae philosophy and physics, though he may have added his own philosophical knowledge to the story. Many modern Romanian authors see Deceneus as a priest who reshaped the worship of Zalmoxis into a popular religion with strict rules.

The Sarmatians represented their 'Ares' as a sword planted upright, and the Scythian and Sarmatian 'Ares' was given blood sacrifices. In the Scythian cult, the throat of one man out of every hundred prisoners was cut and his blood poured on the sword, and his right arm was then cut off and thrown into the air, left wherever it fell. This form of worship continued among the Sarmatians' descendants, the Alans, through the 4th century AD. Jordanes claimed Attila obtained a sacred Scythian sword that had fallen from the sky, the 'Sword of Mars', which he believed made him powerful in war.

Scholars such as Vasile Pârvan argued that the Getae were monotheistic, since ancient sources name no god of the Getae other than Zalmoxis. Yet Herodotus is the only ancient author who explicitly says the Getae had only one divinity, so the debate continues.

Anacharsis was killed by his brother, the Scythian king Saulius, for having sacrificed to the Scythian ancestral Snake-Legged Goddess at her shrine in Hylaea, in an orgiastic and shamanistic night ritual in which he wore images on his dress and played drums. Herodotus claimed instead that Anacharsis was killed for renouncing Scythian customs and adopting Greek ones, but this claim was likely invented by Herodotus himself. His religious rituals corresponded more closely to those of the transvestite Anarya priesthood of the Scythians.

Ancient writers gave the name Zalmoxis a bearskin origin. Porphyrius, in his Vita Pythagorae, says he was so named because he was wrapped in a bearskin at birth, and zalmon is the Thracian word for 'hide'.

Some authors see Zalmoxis as a sky god because the Getae sent him a messenger and shot arrows toward the sky. According to Herodotus, the messenger was chosen by chance every four years and flung into the air onto three upright spears. If he died pierced, the Getae thought the divinity would help them; if he survived, they accused him of being a bad person and sent another. Others suggest Zalmoxis was a chthonic, underworld divinity because of his journey into a cavern.
The Cynics made Anacharsis a favourite figure and ascribed to him a 3rd-century BC work titled the Letters of Anacharsis. Lucian wrote two works about him, Anacharsis or Athletics and The Scythian.

A stele from 104 AD commemorating the Day of Tanais shows the Most High God as a mounted horseman in Sarmatian costume, holding a rhyton. In front of him is a blazing altar and behind it a tree, which represents his communion with the Bosporan Aphrodite Urania.

culture.text: The Sauromatian culture was made up of horse nomads who lived from the lower Volga River to the southern Ural Mountains between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE. No permanent settlements have been found. They are known only from temporary camps and large kurgan tombs.

The Chernyakhov culture flourished between the 2nd and 5th centuries AD across what is now Ukraine, Romania, Moldova and parts of Belarus. It is thought to be a multiethnic mix of Gothic, Geto-Dacian and Sarmatian populations.
The Greek historian Herodotus first mentioned and named the Sauromatian culture. He placed it east of the Don River, 15 days' distance from the northern part of the Sea of Azov.

Outside influences reached the Sauromatian nomads from both directions. Persian Achaemenid influence arrived through Central Asia, most strongly in the north-east during the 6th century BCE. From the 4th century BCE, Greek influence took over, and Greek artifacts appear in nomadic burials as far as the southern Urals.
The Sauromatian culture emerged in the 6th century BCE from elements of the Bronze Age Srubnaya and Andronovo cultures. These were combined with Saka nomadic elements from Central Asia.

The Itkul culture, dated to the 7th to 5th century BCE, was one of the early Saka cultures of the southern Urals. It was based in the eastern foothills and specialized in metallurgy. It was later assimilated into the Early Sarmatian culture.

The Chernyakhov culture was discovered by the Czech-Ukrainian archaeologist Vikentiy Khvoyka, who excavated around Kyiv. It is named after a site near Kyiv, and also after Sântana de Mureș, a cemetery in Transylvania. It replaced the earlier Zarubintsy culture.

Around 370, Huns appeared at the eastern edge of the Chernyakhov culture, and the Gothic leader Ermanaric died. His successor Athanaric found refuge south of the Danube with most of the Gothic population. The culture then declined and was replaced by the Penkovka culture.

At Ossetian feasts, held in honour of a deity, animals are sacrificed and their meat is eaten with ceremonial cheese cakes. Only herbivorous animals such as bulls, rams, goats or lambs are acceptable as sacrifice, and fish are accepted too. As Herodotus attested of the ancient Scythians, the Ossetians, descendants of the Alans, do not sacrifice omnivorous animals like pigs and chickens. Beer and other alcoholic drinks are also generously consumed with each toast, echoing the ancient Scythian custom.

Saka-style deer stones are recorded near the kurgans of Gumarovo in the southern Urals. They are one sign of the strong Eastern influence that spread into the region, mainly through migrations, from the 7th century BCE.

Around 500 BCE, groups from the area of Ancient Khorezm settled in the western southern Urals and were also assimilated into the Early Sarmatians. Nomads of the region are identified by their kurgan burial mounds, such as the Taksai kurgans of about 500 BCE.
